title: Hard times in marriage
hookLine: patience, honesty and forgiveness, with the sangat's help
tomorrow: Jasleen's in her mother-in-law's kitchen. what's in the pot?

cards: It starts over a grocery receipt, the way these things do. Jasleen picked up extra shifts. Aman, still job hunting, said something sharp about who's paying for what, and then both of them said worse.

Now it's Friday night, Jasleen is at Bebe's kitchen table with red eyes, and two people who love her disagree about what she should do next. Her mother-in-law has already called: come home, we'll all sit down together.
Jasleen says no. This stays between me and him.

teach.b: Let both sides speak. Jasleen's case: honesty starts between the two people in the marriage.

Bring the families in too soon and everyone takes a side, the fight gets an audience, and the couple never learns to repair it alone. Her mother-in-law's case: nobody in Sikhi is meant to carry a burden alone.

teach.h: IN-LAWS: THE SANGAT HOLDS YOU UP.
teach.b: The sangat, the community, exists to hold people up, and elders who have weathered their own marriages can see what two tired people can't. Both of those are real, and both sit inside the tradition.
What both sides share is the slow work underneath.

teach.h: FARID, ANG 1384: PATIENCE IS THE BOW.
teach.b: On ang 1384, Baba Farid, whose verses are in the Granth, makes patience the whole bow: patience the bow, patience the string, patience the arrow, in paraphrase, and God won't let that arrow miss.
And on ang 1372, Kabir says where there is forgiveness, there is God himself. Notice it doesn't say forgiveness goes to whoever started it. One thing isn't up for debate.

If a home is ever unsafe, patience isn't the answer: get somewhere safe and call local emergency help, or 988 in the US if anyone is thinking of self-harm. Jasleen's fight isn't that. It's two scared people and a receipt.
Bebe pours her tea and doesn't take a side.

how: Sikh couples facing hard times may do Ardas together, seek counsel from trusted elders or the sangat, and lean on Gurbani about patience and forgiveness; a home that is not safe calls for real help, not endurance.

games.q: what does “hard times in marriage” mean?
o: a sign the couple chose the wrong partner
a private matter the Gurus never speak about
trouble met with patience, honesty and forgiveness

games.q: two voices, one table — tap the pairs.
p: honesty between the two of us first
where forgiveness is, there is God

s: Sikh teaching says to keep marriage troubles hidden from everyone
the sangat exists to hold people up; when to bring it in is the real debate.
Kabir's line ties forgiveness to God's presence
where there is forgiveness, there is God himself.
patience means staying in a home that isn't safe
if a home is unsafe, get somewhere safe and call for help; patience isn't the answer to danger.

games.q: your brother and his wife fight, and you think the family should step in. before you say so, state his wife's best case for keeping it between the two of them.
o: a couple has to learn to repair alone, and an audience makes everyone take sides.
families never help; they only gossip about the fight afterward.
it's nobody's business, because marriage has nothing to do with the sangat.
games.why: a fair debate starts with the other side at its best. hers: honesty begins between two. the family's: nobody carries it alone. patience and forgiveness sit under both.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing someone at home did that still stings a little: a tone, a forgotten errand, a dish left in the sink. Say quietly, out loud if you can, I'm letting this one go.
Then let it go with your next breath out, and sit.

wordCard.voice: Hard times in marriage. Met in Sikhi with patience, honesty and forgiveness, and the sangat's help when it's needed.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: khima, forgiveness; Kabir on ang 1372: where there is forgiveness, there is God.

carryVoice: Patience at home: the bow, the string and the arrow, and forgiveness that doesn't wait to see who started it. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 1384 (Salok Farid: sabar man kamaan e sabar kaa neehnoo, sabar sandaa baan), paraphrased
Ang 1372 (Salok Kabir: jahaa daiaa tah dharam hai... jahaa khimaa tah aap), paraphrased
